kind.note: The magazine selector supplies the existing brick/open-roof family. The construction_site opt-in replaces its uniform magazine walls and painted door with thick, partly raised walls, real work openings and interior timber stages. It makes no claim that this hotel was a magazine. The opt-in is restricted to a one-storey roofless brick worksite and leaves garrison models on their existing builders.

construction.note: THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS STRUCTURE'S FABRIC THAT IS DOCUMENTED, and it is documented in the source's own words: 'This hotel, WHICH WAS BUILT OF BRICK, was three stories and a basement in height' (Andreas, transcribed on chicagology_prefire112, and confirmed in the printed volume). The uncredited paragraph on the same page repeats 'built of brick'. It is also locally plausible rather than merely asserted: Tyler K. Blodgett established Chicago's first brickyard on the North Side in the spring of 1833 (docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.12; data/structures/brickyard_north_side.json). NOTE WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED BY IT: that any brick had been laid by 1835-07-01. Andreas describes the FINISHED hotel of 1836. The material is carried into the scene-date shell as an inference about continuity of intention, which is a small step and still a step.

period_brick.note: T-3387: laid in K03's lake-clay brick (`soft_mud_salmon_lake`): Chicago's own first brick, from Blodgett's North Side yard of 1833, which the record traces this building's brick to; the local lake clay is high in lime and burns salmon to buff, not red. The shade, the bond and that the Lake House's brick came from that yard's clay are the reconstruction (L-k03-period-brick-3387).

stories.note: One partially raised working storey is a reconstructed July 1835 choice within a zero-to-two-storey range, not a measured schedule. The 10 June notice attests active work; Bonnell retrospectively describes construction under a conflicting 1835/1836/1837 date, Martineau describes unfinished work in June 1836, and Andreas gives an autumn 1836 opening. These bound an unfinished project but cannot select the July lift. The model chooses one incomplete lift without a roof or completed-hotel fittings.

wall_height_m.note: The maximum working-front wall is 4.0 m; other lifts step down to 1.2–3.28 m. These are reconstructed bounds inherited from the earlier four-metre shell, not measured basement or storey heights. The worksite remains below the later three-storey completed hotel, and no uniform four-metre enclosure is implied.

roof_type.note: Reconstructed open-shell choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June notice establishes work before the scene but dates no roof or lift. Neither the June 1836 unfinished interior nor autumn opening proves July roof absence. Roof none omits all caps; the worksite is built openly at the reconstructed tier. The later Kellogg print shows a completed roof and cupola in ca.1836–1849 and is ineligible to prescribe the July construction stage.

paint.note: The archetype's `paint` names the wall's surface finish, not a coat of paint, and 'brick' is the value that lets the documented brick fabric read as brick. It is inferred rather than documented because nothing describes the surface of this building at any date: bare brick is the ordinary finish and the alternative - stuccoed or whitewashed - is not excluded by anything, though it would be an odd thing to do to an unfinished shell.

chimneys.note: NOT A COUNT OF THE FINISHED HOTEL'S STACKS, which nobody records, but a consequence of the state: a shell one storey up has no chimneys standing above it. The archetype places stacks against the ridge, and this structure has no ridge. Inferred from the construction state rather than from any statement.

construction_site.note: A bounded July 1835 worksite, not a reconstruction of the completed hotel. The 10 June Chicago Democrat notice establishes a house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. No source measures the July progress. Within the existing 24 × 15 m plan and 4 m maximum, 0.46 m thick brick walls now step down from the higher north working front to the lower rear lift. Seven selected work bays have real unglazed openings and only the first three have their brickwork bridged above reconstructed timber lintels; a broad rear break admits material. Two short timber working stages stand inside the shell. Bay count, wall thickness, lift heights, apertures, staging stock and placement are reconstructed working choices, not features traced from the later print. The existing external brick, timber and footing-stone piles remain separately declared in the yard layer. No excavation or below-grade interior is represented. L-lake-house-worksite-2379.

function.note:
The building's purpose is documented and its completion date is documented, and between them they make the scene-date function a construction site rather than a hotel. Andreas: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House ... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836, Jacob Russel, of Middleton, Conn., assuming control of its management.' The men behind it are documented too and are worth carrying because they are the town's commercial leadership rather than innkeepers: Gurdon S. Hubbard, General David S. Hunter, John H. Kinzie, Dr W. B. Egan and Major James B. Campbell - 'the men whose enterprise led them into building a house which for those days was far in advance of the needs of the town'.

AND THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS DATES THE SITE, WHICH ANDREAS DOES NOT. 'There is [a] new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake Hous[e]."' — the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001, the same paragraph that reports the Sauganash freshly refitted. Both halves are load-bearing. IT IS A BUILDING SITE three weeks before the scene date, north of the main branch, which is what makes hotel_under_construction an attested function at 1835-07-01 rather than a back-projection from the 1836 opening. AND ITS NAME IS STILL SECOND-HAND — 'we understand' — so on the scene date the town has an unfinished building that people are calling the Lake House and not a hotel with a sign. The same paragraph contains an editorial proposal for a house 'about double the size of that latter' near the centre of Lake Street on this side of the river. The comparison expresses a desired relative hotel size; it supplies no measured dimensions or July construction stage and does not establish the Lake House's rank among existing buildings. The proposal is not an existing-house observation and does not prove that the suggested site was vacant.

Fergus's 1876 recollection of the 1839 hotel is included here only for later establishment identity and the conflicting Rush/North Water address, not as evidence of the July 1835 construction stage, position or dimensions. Its Hotels entry was directly checked at the printed page; the existing contemporary project notice remains the evidence for work before the scene date.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by Robert A Kenzie, 7 May 1831
land_owner.note: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (`e1834_harbor_cut/shoreline.geojson`), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land_sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 51 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

placement.position_note: THE THREE STREETS ARE DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS; WHICH SIDE OF RUSH STREET IS NOT DOCUMENTED AT ALL, AND THAT IS WHY THIS POSITION IS CONJECTURAL RATHER THAN INFERRED. Andreas in the hotel chapter: 'located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter'. Andreas in his account of the First Unitarian Society, whose first Chicago service was held in the unfinished building in June 1836: 'The services were held in the Lake House, WHICH STOOD AT THE CORNER OF RUSH AND MICHIGAN STREETS.' Two chapters, one corner, and no side. A block between Kinzie and Michigan has two faces on Rush, about 110 m apart, and nothing reached says which one this is; the east side is adopted because the backers' own ground - Kinzie's Addition - and the north-bank commercial group Bonnell describes east of Rush lie that way, which is an argument about a neighbourhood and not evidence about a building. IF IT IS WRONG THE BUILDING BELONGS ABOUT 110 M WEST. A SECOND AND LARGER TRAP IS IN THE STREET NAME ITSELF. 'Michigan Street' on the north side in 1835 is the east-west street one block north of Kinzie - today's East Hubbard Street - and it is NOT Michigan Avenue, which did not cross the river until 1920. chicagology_prefire112's uncredited paragraph glosses the site as 'near where the Wrigley Building stands today', and the Wrigley Building stands on Michigan AVENUE at the river, about 150 m south-east of the block Andreas's three streets describe and on the wrong side of Kinzie. docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.8 carries the same gloss and additionally renders the third street as 'Michigan (Water)', equating it with North Water Street, which no source reached supports. This record follows Andreas's street names and records the gloss as the error it appears to be. METHOD: the modern East Hubbard Street / North Rush Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448121.71, N 4637764.21 (OSM node 261149251, fetched 2026-08-11); the building's north face is set on the Michigan Street frontage 12.2 m south of it and its west face on the Rush frontage 12.2 m east of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Michigan Street, which is the one orientation Andreas does state - 'fronting on the latter'. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), plus the block width if the side of Rush is wrong, plus whatever a building site's outline means when the building is not finished. NO SOURCES ARE CITED ON THIS ATTRIBUTE, deliberately: the streets are quoted in this note and are Andreas's, but the COORDINATE turns on a side of Rush Street that no source states, and a citation on a conjectural position would be decorative. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS MODELLED - the e1834_harbor_cut heightfield now runs local E -320..+1700 and N -400..+400, and this footprint at E +1061.2..+1085.2, N +341.2..+356.2 lands on it within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground_contact declaration. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED is the excavation: a construction site is a hole in the ground before it is anything else, and this project has no way to cut a cellar into the terrain, so the shell sits ON the surface rather than in it.
placement.symbolic_location: North side of the river in Kinzie's Addition, on the block between Kinzie Street and Michigan Street east of Rush Street (today between East Kinzie Street and East Hubbard Street east of North Rush Street), fronting north onto Michigan Street.

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

stories.note: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

construction.note: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log_core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

log_core.note: Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow claimed the Green Tree was originally of logs and weatherboarded only years later. Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

cladding.note: Not directly attested for this building. Clapboard is the standard cladding for a frame building of this type and period, and the competing log-core account calls the covering 'weatherboarding', which is the same thing under another name — so both readings of the construction converge on a lapped horizontal board exterior.

paint.note: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

wall_height_m.note: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

roof_type.note: John Gray: 'There should also be a small attic window in the gable end, for we used the attic, too.' A gable end with a window in it is a direct attestation of the roof form — one of the few in this dataset that is not typological. With the front on Canal and the long side on Lake, the gable ends face east and west and the ridge runs east-west along Lake Street.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing and leaves an attic tall enough to lodge people in, which the sources say it did.

fenestration.note: The PANE CHARACTER is attested — a guest chamber 'about 12x12, with two windows 6x8', small-paned sash, plus 'a small attic window in the gable end'. Two windows per 12 ft chamber on a 40 x 25 ft two-storey block implies a regularly fenestrated elevation. Since T-0083 the ARRANGEMENT is carried by elevation_scheme, read off plate '11'; this value still states the pane character, which the plate agrees with — 6-over-6 sash in even bays.

elevation_scheme.note: THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN ALONG THE EAVES ELEVATIONS. Two halves, separately grounded. That the front is a gable end is a join of attested facts already in this record: the front on Canal (F. H. Taylor), the long side on Lake, and the gable ends facing east and west (John Gray's attic window note, and the roof_type note's own reading). The bay ARRANGEMENT — even 6-over-6 sash in regular bays along the long elevation, doors and attic lights on the gable faces — is read off plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set, committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png: a tier-5 retrospective view, which may drive fenestration rhythm as inferred and may never drive a coordinate. The plate is not yet held as a source record (T-0075 owns that), so the citation is a committed path. The pictured south eaves elevation's bay count is now stated separately by eaves_bays on T-2376; the opposite elevation keeps the archetype's footprint arithmetic as a reconstruction under docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. No dimension or geographic placement is taken from the plate.

side_entrance.note: PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL, not a finding that this inn never had a side door. The held Andreas/Braunhold reproduction shows seven sash on the south long elevation on each floor, with a sash at the middle ground-floor station. The independently held original Trowbridge plate in Gale 1902, facing p.35 / scan n55, captioned 'The Green Tree Tavern in 1835', shows the same seven-bay window rhythm and no middle ground-floor door; its frontmost lower sash is partly obscured by the hanging board and people, while the middle station is visible. Setting this existing attribute to null selects the archetype's normal sash at all seven existing south-wall stations instead of substituting a door at the fourth station. The earlier John Gray testimony is retained here verbatim: 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side', with the hall and stairway behind it (chicagology_prefire127, transcribing the Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883; Gray kept the inn in 1838-41). That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. Existing south-wall seven-bay count, even spacing, stock sash dimensions and height bands, north-wall rhythm, primary front entrance, footprint, geographic placement and all other form values stay unchanged. No c.1859 check_required photograph or Gray-derived new geometry supplies this correction; the two public-domain picture records supply the visible sash pattern.

chimney_placement.note: END CHIMNEYS AT BOTH GABLES. Plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set (committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png, and its sibling Braunhold view written up as image 6 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) draws one stack at each end of the ridge — a tier-5 retrospective view driving massing as inferred. The plates are not yet held as source records (T-0075), so the citation is a committed path. This replaces the archetype's frontage-fraction arrangement, which on this deeper-than-wide footprint had left both stacks standing OFF the ridge on the roof slopes — the before frame of T-0083 shows it. The COUNT stays the chimneys attribute's own inference; docs/LIBERTIES.md L21 (the town chimney arrangement) and L152 say what is invented here.

rear_ell.note:
T-2376 retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction choice. Its original position was a reconstruction made under the obsolete Canal placement, using the pictured lower wing and Gray's later testimony without a dated rear plan. The governing drawings do not resolve or show that projecting right/rear form. Gray explicitly recalls a right addition 'the same as on the left' during his 1838–41 tenancy, and the historical note promised a second wing if the Lake-and-West-Water placement won; that later bilateral testimony and the promise remain counterevidence, not proof that either addition was absent in 1835 or that both were the same pictured building. The revised model builds the pictured left connector/range, keeps the competing shoulder readings, and leaves an unverified 1835 rear/bilateral stage unmodeled rather than presenting the old placement proxy as another established wing. No historic absence, alteration date, tenant identity or room count is asserted.

HISTORICAL PRE-RETIREMENT NOTE:
THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. John Gray, landlord 1838-41, attests 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left'; the 1838 Braunhold engraving (owner_brief_2026_08_18 README, image 6) draws 'a lower gabled wing at the left with a wide (carriage) door', and plate '11' (prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png) draws the low gabled wing with the ship masts behind it. WHETHER A WING STOOD ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray describes the house three to six years after the scene date — so this is a reconstruction under the owner's 2026-08-18 standing ruling, sized by the views and claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. WHY THE REAR END AND ONLY THE REAR: Gray names additions at BOTH ends, but this record's committed placement puts the west face ON Canal Street's east frontage with zero offset, so the street end has no ground to build on — only the east (rear, yard) end does. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

gallery.note: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. The witnesses describe two entrances — the front on Canal and one 'about the middle of the long side' on Lake — without mentioning a porch, veranda or gallery, which is weak negative evidence at best, since they were correcting a drawing rather than inventorying the elevation. False is the default, not a finding. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) settles this the moment anyone opens it.

side_additions.note: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the house: 'There should also be a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left.' So by the end of the 1830s the two-storey core had a low single-storey addition at each end. WHETHER THEY EXISTED ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray's testimony describes the building three to six years after the scene date — which is why this is inferred and why the additions stay out of the footprint polygon. SINCE T-0083 the rear (east) one is BUILT, at the reconstructed tier, as form.rear_ell — see that attribute for why only the rear end has ground to build on. This value stays the testimony record for BOTH ends; the street-end addition remains unbuilt.

chimneys.note: Not attested in text. A tavern with a bar-room at one end, a parlour, a dining room clearable for dancing and chambers above needed more than one fireplace, and two stacks is the normal disposition for a 40 ft block with a central hall. The number is inference — and since T-0083 it agrees with plate '11', which draws exactly two. WHERE they stand is carried by chimney_placement.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

eaves_bays.note: Seven opening stations are drawn on the visible long elevation in the public-domain Andreas/Braunhold plate, held locally as chicago/reference/images/chicago/chicago_green_tree_inn_1838.jpg; the seven upper sash centres are approximately x 822, 928, 1041, 1146, 1243, 1347 and 1443 in its 1600-pixel-wide reproduction. This is tier-5 retrospective form evidence, not a dimension, coordinate or demonstrated 1835 elevation. The existing west-facing gable and Lake Street south-side reading assign that pictured long wall to local x_min; no position or footprint changes. The opposite x_max face is not overridden and retains its six-bay reconstruction. Seven bays fit the existing 12.19 m length at about 1.74 m per bay, keeping the archetype's existing 0.85 m sash and 1.35 m height. Their equal spacing, vertical bands and hidden treatment remain reconstructed. The earlier form replaced the middle lower sash with Gray's textually described south-side entrance. The current T-2376 picture-priority choice uses the existing side_entrance:null option to retain that seventh sash. Gray's later entrance recollection remains explicit counterevidence: no alteration date or absence of that door on 1 July 1835 is established. Other gable, wing and attic-light differences are classified in the individual picture match records.

gable_wall_cladding.note: The pictured main gable continues the framed wall’s horizontal clapboard above the eaves; it is not roof covering. The main-block end triangles now use the existing wall finish and existing reconstructed siding course stock. This switch covers both main gables for a closed model: continuing the pictured finish around the unseen/opposite end is reconstructed, not independently attested. Existing footprint, placement, eave/ridge geometry, roof pitch and covering, course stock and all subsidiary roofs remain unchanged. It does not settle the provisional camera or any remaining opening, roof, wing or grouped-annex differences.

front_ground_layout.note: Two sash left of a rightmost front-gable entrance agree in the actually viewed Andreas 1884 p634/n1301 plate, Trowbridge/Gale 1902 plate facing p35/n55, and Kurz & Allison 1893 panel11. This is retrospective form agreement, not independent contemporaneous proof of 1 July 1835; Kurz may derive from Andreas and Trowbridge may rely on later material. The ascending LOCAL-u fractions are door .20, sash .50, sash .78: exterior +y viewers see higher u toward screen left, so this yields two screen-left sash and a screen-right entrance. Exact centre fractions .20/.50/.78 across the existing 7.62 m wall, equal existing .85x1.35 m sash and 1.20x2.10 m door stock, sill bands, sections and hidden joinery are RECONSTRUCTED, not measured or attested by those pictures. Only the +y front ground floor opts in. The current two upper sash versus Trowbridge's three, attic light, text-attested south-side door, disputed additions, roof, geographic placement and all existing source/camera uncertainties stay unresolved. The held-rights/unverified 1859 source is excluded as a geometry witness. Original T-2376 remains open/differs; this is not a solved camera or picture match. The same pure resolved_front_ground_stations dataclass property (whose actual values are covered by the existing native mesh recipe) is consumed by the mesh and the native entrance/apron/clearance reader after resolving exactly the sidecar-selected source phase; no renderer facade API or bearing is changed. AMENDMENT 2026-11-10: the earlier statement calling two upper sash versus Trowbridge three unresolved is superseded by form.front_upper_layout. The omission is being physically corrected as three upper stations, not closed by a camera/tolerance label; genuine follow-up native and three source rerenders remain required.

enclosed_left_annex.note:
CURRENT CLOSED-SHOULDER WORKING READING: Andreas's detailed retrospective engraving supplies a closed clapboard shoulder with a lower sash and small front-gable light, followed by a low connector and farther turned gabled range. The existing shoulder_enclosed option is now true. Trowbridge/Gale's captioned1835 drawing instead shows an open post-and-roof wagon bay. That remains explicit counterevidence, not a demonstrated conversion year; the current choice is an evidence-bounded reconstruction of the July1835 scene. The independently drawn open shed/posts and its covered wagon are declined together by the yard source owner while this same canonical attribute is true, rather than drawn inside the closed shoulder.

 Every metric span, hidden depth, height, slope, opening station/section, local placement, plan turn, timber and colour choice remains exactly the existing reconstructed group. No new number, measured plan, surveyed coordinate, historical interior, occupant or extra lodging capacity is inferred. The main footprint and world placement are unchanged. The actual fixed-camera comparison now includes the closed wall, sash and dormer; left-cluster roof silhouette and relative proportions still differ. Original T-2376 remains open/differs. The earlier open-bay model rationale is preserved verbatim in docs/RESEARCH/green-tree-annex-T-2376/previous-open-reading-20261103.md.

 SHOULDER DORMER CAP, 2026-11-04: front_gable_peak_m is raised 4.50 to 4.85 m so the little front-gable light over the closed shoulder reads as the sharply pointed cap Andreas draws, rather than the blunt, nearly flat cap the 4.50 m value produced. Against the builder's existing 4.20 m dormer head and its 0.625 m roof half-span that turns the cap from about 25.6 to about 46.1 degrees. 4.85 m is a RECONSTRUCTED working control chosen for the drawn triangular shape; it is not a measurement off the retrospective plate, which carries no scale, dimension or camera, and it dates nothing. Nothing else moves: the peak stays below the unchanged 5.0 m main-wall head, and the dormer plan extent, the light, the lower sash, the connector, the turned range, the main block, the footprint and the world placement are untouched. The shoulder roof silhouette and the left group's relative proportions remain OPEN on T-2376.

 SHOULDER ROOF RISE TRIAL, 2026-11-09: the existing roof_high_m working control rises from 4.0 to 4.6 m at the main-block attachment, retaining the outer roof_low_m 3.2 m. Across the unchanged 3.6 m shoulder span this steepens the shed from about 12.5 to 21.3 degrees, following the stronger rise toward the main wall visible behind the little pointed light in Andreas. These are RECONSTRUCTED trial controls for relative form, not dimensions measured from the retrospective drawing, and establish no historical alteration or July-1835 stage. The accepted 4.85 m pointed cap, its light and lower sash, the 2.8 m shoulder wall, all three component spans/depths/occupied polygons and their turn, the main building and its surveyed placement remain unchanged. Existing source disagreement with Trowbridge’s open bay remains explicit. The actual new native mesh, unchanged-camera comparison and published compound review are still required; original T-2376 remains open and the broader left-group proportions are not signed off by this one slope trial.

T-2376 WHOLE LEFT GROUP, 2026-11-10: rereading the actual verified public-domain Andreas and Kurz pictures reveals two distinct far-left gable peaks: the low foreground range and a higher rear gable behind it. The former single constant-height range omitted that visible shape. A bounded rear raised roof section now sits inside the same range envelope, with reconstructed 1.6 m rear depth, 4.5 m wall and 37 degree roof; the front retains its existing 2.6 m wall and 37 degree roof. The existing range depth increases 3.0 to 3.7 m and its front set-out 1.0 to 1.7 m together, retaining the rear corner and 25 degree turn, bringing the low foreground gable forward. The low connector roof now falls away from the main block toward that foreground range, following the pictured link instead of the previous reversed wedge; its working upper edge is 3.0 m and lower edge remains 2.25 m. Existing stock clapboard continues over the shoulder and link upper infill, where the old proxy left a plain patch. Every new metric is RECONSTRUCTED, chosen for bounded relative form rather than measured from a retrospective picture; no historical alteration date, extra room or occupant, site move, new surveyed outline or grade is asserted. Andreas and Kurz may be dependent; Trowbridge’s competing open bay and upper/attic count, Gray’s later side entrance and bilateral additions, and the held c1859 catalogue lead remain explicit counterevidence. Final native/source pictures and actual app review are owed before acceptance; the old partial statements above are historical, not current blockers by themselves. The same original-ticket whole-picture reading lowers the existing foreground range upper-light sill from3.1 to2.7m, retaining its0.65x0.70m section; this is a reconstructed placement within the low gable, not a measured sash height.

front_upper_layout.note: THREE UPPER FRONT SASH, T-2376 categorical omission correction. Direct review of the actual native9dd Trowbridge pair shows the model has two upper main-gable sash where the verified public-domain 1902 illustration clearly draws three. The earlier two-versus-three tolerance classification is withdrawn: this is a missing opening and remains OPEN until the genuine corrected native is rendered and reviewed. Andreas and Kurz show two fully legible upper sash plus a narrow/partly obscured left-edge detail at the shoulder junction; that earlier reading did not safely establish a historic two-window row. Adopt the clearly pictured three-station Trowbridge row as an evidence-bounded reconstruction for the early inn, without inventing an alteration date or declaring three independent contemporary witnesses. The chosen local-u fractions .20/.50/.78 match the existing ground stations, with the existing .85x1.35m sash and upper sill/head band retained. Those fractions, exact stock dimensions, trim, even vertical alignment and July1835 continuity are RECONSTRUCTED, not measured from the drawing. Only the main +y upper row changes: ground door/sash, rear and eaves rows, attic lights, completed left group, footprint, geographic placement and source rights/grades stay unchanged. No held c1859 photograph or site1859 engraving supplies geometry.

function.note: In operation as a public house throughout the scene window: bar-room serving as office and reception, dining room cleared for dancing, chambers above and lodging in the attic when full. Renamed the Chicago Hotel by 1844, which is after the scene date and is a change of sign, not of trade.

occupants.note: Ingersoll's tenancy is given as 1834-1837, which covers 1835-07-01, with Martin M. Ford associated. DRLOIH's list — 'initially by David Clark and then by Edward Parsons' — carries no dates and is compatible rather than contradictory: Clark (or Clock) is named elsewhere as the landlord who opened the house in 1833, before Ingersoll.

placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.
placement.symbolic_location: North-east corner of Lake Street and West Water Street, on the west bank of the South Branch; the long elevation on Lake, the front west onto West Water, the river end on the bank as far as the modelled ground carries it.

stories.note: THIS VALUE IS THE LOG CORE'S, AND UNTIL 2026-08-10 IT CARRIED THE FRAME RANGE'S. It read 'value 2, documented', with a note saying in as many words that the two storeys described the river-fronting range rather than the whole building — but `log_dwelling` reads `stories` as the storey count of the log core, the range having its own `frame_addition_stories`, so the documented claim was being spent on the cabin and the range then took the archetype's default. The result was the composition inverted: a two-storey log cabin standing behind a shorter frame block, which is the opposite of every description of this building. The two-storey claim now sits on `frame_addition_stories`, where the archetype reads it and where the source's sentence actually points. ONE STOREY FOR THE CABIN IS INFERENCE, not attestation: no source gives the log part a height, and the reading rests on the 1833 view from the south bank — 'a two-story building and adjoining log cabin' — which only reads as a contrast if the cabin stood lower, together with the single-pen log house being the near-universal form at the forks. Recorded rather than assumed, because the number the archetype builds from should be the number a reader can argue with.

construction.note: chicagology: 'It was a log structure partly sided, and was erected by Mr. Samuel Miller.' The value records the log core; the frame range in front is carried separately as frame_addition. 'Partly sided' and 'a two-story house added to the cabin' are the same building described from two angles and are not in conflict.

frame_addition.note: A two-storey house added to the log cabin, fronting the river. This is the element that faced the settlement across the water and the one a viewer standing at Wolf Point would have seen. THAT IT EXISTED IS DOCUMENTED AND ITS SIZE IS NOT, so the four attributes below state the side, the width, the depth and the storey count explicitly rather than leaving them to the archetype's defaults. Until 2026-08-10 they were left to the defaults, which is the failure docs/LIBERTIES.md L24 exists to stop one building over: a documented feature arriving at an invented size with nothing admitting it.

frame_addition_side.note: The cleared1867 retrospective1833 drawing shows the low log front beside the two-storey range. The kit's end option places the tall block beside the low core. This replaces the earlier attested front claim: the text 'fronting the river' describes facade orientation and does not establish that the tall block stood physically ahead of the cabin; the old note had mistaken that interpretation for attestation. Pictured adjacent form is inferred; exact plan dimensions and July1835 continuity remain as separately graded. The existing river-facing bearing is retained.

frame_addition_stories.note: 'added a TWO-STORY house to the cabin, fronting the river', with the 1833 view's 'a two-story building and adjoining log cabin' saying the same thing from the south bank. This is the storey count the sources actually give, and until 2026-08-10 it was recorded on `stories`, where the archetype spent it on the log core instead; see the note there.

frame_addition_width_m.note: RECONSTRUCTED: retained9 m width of the tall range, not a dimension measured from the picture. The explicit15 m native union leaves6 m for the adjacent low core. Exact front opening stations and roof span remain reconstructed proxies.

frame_addition_depth_m.note: RECONSTRUCTED: retained6 m depth of the tall range. The current kit's end addition shares that6 m depth with a6 m-wide low core, giving a literal90 m2 rectangular union. The source supports adjacent differing-height forms, not any of these metre choices.

frame_addition_cladding.note: The tall Miller House at the right of the inspected 1867 Wolf's Point in 1833 lithograph has exposed horizontal log courses downstairs and vertical boards on its upper storey and gable. This replaces the generator's default horizontal clapboard over both storeys; the source is a retrospective pictured-form witness, not a survey or proof of unchanged appearance on 1 July 1835. The existing two-storey 5.2 m addition height is retained. Its midpoint at 2.6 m is a reconstructed floor/cladding break; the board-edge rhythm, narrow relief and exact joint treatment are reconstructed proxies under L-miller-mixed-cladding-2381. The adjacent lower wing, explicit front openings and independent roof pitches now follow the pictured composition under the qualified image review; dimensions, hidden construction and the low core stack retain their separate uncertainty. ACTUAL-RENDER FOLLOW-UP: the first same-material 12 mm edge/12 mm relief treatment was visually ineffective. Joint proxies now use 24 mm width and 4 mm relief with the existing darker log material, at the retained nominal 0.24 m board rhythm. These are reconstructed graphic joint cues, not measured historic board gaps, raised battens, a painted finish or surveyed joinery; their faces remain confidence 1.0.

frame_addition_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 5.2 m is about 17 ft: two storeys at typical period floor heights plus structure and a sill. THIS IS THE HEIGHT THIS RECORD HAS CARRIED SINCE 2026-08-09, moved to the element it was written about — it sat on `wall_height_m`, which the archetype applies to the log core, and the note there said so and flagged the overstatement because the archetype could not then express two heights. It can, so the value moves rather than staying flagged. Stated explicitly instead of taking the archetype's 4.7 m default for two storeys, so that the reasoning already recorded for this building is what the mesh is built from.

wall_height_m.note: THE LOG CABIN'S WALL, not the frame range's. No figure is attested for either. 2.6 m is a single-pen log wall at the forks — the same height this record has named for the cabin since 2026-08-09, when it stood in this note as the height the archetype could not yet express while the field itself carried the range's 5.2 m. The two heights are now separate attributes, so the overstatement this note used to flag is gone rather than described: docs/LIBERTIES.md L13, the entry that recorded it, moves to Resolved with this slice.

roof_type.note: Not attested for this building. Gable is the near-universal roof form for both elements of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: The governing lithograph and inspected held variants consistently show the low wing's roof rising less above its wall than the tall range's roof.25 degrees is a reconstructed first fit for the6 m-deep core, giving about1.40 m rise over its2.6 m wall. Neither the angle nor either metre is measured from the drawing. The independent frame-addition override retains the tall roof's preceding38-degree proxy; no authentic July1835 pitch is asserted. The genuine final native comparison follows that relative lower-roof form under the visitor stopping rule; it does not turn the reconstructed angle into a historical measurement.

cladding.note: The earlier inference of clapboard from the text 'partly sided' is superseded for the tall block by the actual 1867 lithograph: log courses on its lower storey, vertical boards upstairs and on the gable. The consumed the addition's exterior covering parameter now builds that distinction. The original cabin remains log. Numeric course/board dimensions and unseen elevations retain their reconstructed treatment; a retrospective view does not settle the building's exact July 1835 condition.

paint.note: No source describes a finish. Unpainted is the default reading and is positively supported by Wau-Bun's account of the Sauganash's white paint being the admiration of the little circle at Wolf Point in 1831 — the Miller house was directly across the water from it and is not singled out that way.

chimneys.note: The count remains the existing inference of one stack per element. The 1867 Blanchard/Shober retrospective 1833 view visibly shows a short flue penetrating the tall range's ridge; frame_addition_ridge_stack records that inferred form. Its exact station and section are reconstructed. The separate low cabin's stack is not resolved in that view and retains its existing inferred exterior placement, not a pictured claim or an absence finding.

frame_addition_ridge_stack.note: The cleared1867 lithograph labelled1833 supports a short head penetrating the tall range's ridge. The retained tuple[0.40,0.45,0.46] is reconstructed: fractional station, square width and head above ridge are proxy choices, not survey measurements. The main roof retains38 degrees through the independent addition override and the stack foot uses that pitch. Switching to the existing end route trims the buried roof edge and shifts the fractional station0.156 m, below the visitor-noticeable size/place bar. The low core's existing inferred stack and count of two remain; other held pictures do not resolve that core stack clearly enough to establish absence. No unchanged July1835 detail is attested. The actual source gate caught the earlier 0.450 m head below the documented eighteen-inch (0.4572 m) minimum. Its reconstructed head is now 0.460 m, a 10 mm correction below the visitor-noticeable picture threshold; the source does not measure this height.

frame_addition_front_set_out.note: The tall front retains the same six opening rectangles as the preceding revised model: lower window-door-window and three upper windows. Their counts and pictured arrangement are inferred from the cleared1867 retrospective1833 lithograph; all metric stations, widths, heights and floor bands are reconstructed. Local coordinates are relative to the addition's own -x edge. This explicit set-out replaces the separate upper-row count control and adds the source-like ground door independently of that count. The opposite-quarter camera reveals the correct gable quarter; no exact historical camera station or unchanged July1835 condition is attested.

front_set_out.note: The low wing's long front carries one door toward its far end and one small window beside the tall range, following the cleared1867 drawing. In the retained opposite-quarter diagnostic, local -x projects screen-right: the door at1.8 m is farther right and the window at4.5 m is nearer the tall block. Pictured presence/count is inferred; these stations, stock sections,1.95 m heads and the exact6 m width are reconstructed. The existing one-storey log-front set-out consumer is extended only to an end-addition core; it does not remove the main range's own front door.

frame_addition_roof_pitch_deg.note: Retains the tall range's existing38-degree roof proxy while the low core uses its own lower reconstructed25-degree first fit. The override also supplies the addition ridge-flue's roof-run foot calculation, so its foot stays under the same roof plane. This preserves the main roof angle, not every endpoint vertex: the kit's existing end-addition route trims0.26 m at the buried joint and shifts the same fractional flue station by0.156 m; exact historic endpoints/stations are unmeasured, and neither change is a new historical claim.

function.note: NOT AN INN AT THE SCENE DATE, and that is the most important fact this record carries. Miller's tavern competed with the Wolf Point Tavern from 1830, but Wau-Bun, describing 1831, already calls the Miller house 'at this time vacant', Miller having removed to the place that was becoming Michigan City; DRLOIH has the business converted to a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832; and a third account has Miller retiring from the field in 1834. The three disagree in their chronology and agree in their direction. Modelled as present and in secondary store or residential use, not innkeeping. The specific claim that Peck was running it does not survive to the scene date either — this project's own exclusions record places Peck in 1835 at his two-storey frame store at South Water and LaSalle.

stated_use.note: EVERY OCCUPANT ANY SOURCE NAMES BELONGS TO AN EARLIER YEAR. Wau-Bun, describing 1831, calls the Miller house 'at this time vacant', Miller having removed towards Michigan City. DRLOIH has the business turned into a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832, and this project's own date guards place Peck in 1835 at his frame store at South Water and LaSalle instead. A third account has Miller leaving the field in 1834. The accounts agree that the house stood past its innkeeping days, in store or residential use. None places a person in it on 1 July 1835. hh_miller_samuel carries no address for the same reason. So the roof states its use and the gap rather than seating a guess.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BUILDING — the streets platted across this ground in Kinzie's Addition were staked in 1833-35 and the point itself has since been rebuilt — so the coordinate is derived from the datum origin at the forks confluence and from bank geometry. What is attested is unusually consistent for this dataset: chicagology, 'The Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the Main Channel'; Wau-Bun, 'on the north side of the river ... near the forks'; DRLOIH, a store 'on the north bank of the river at the forks'; and the Miller-Clybourn ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point Tavern, which requires it to be on the point. A FOURTH SOURCE DISAGREES AND IS TREATED AS AN ERROR: the hotel chronology places Miller on the 'south branch of Chicago River, opposite Wolf Point'. Four independent statements against one, and the ferry route settles it. Method: modern water polygons from OpenStreetMap put the nose of the point at about 39 m north of the datum origin, with the main-stem north bank running east from there and the North Branch east bank running north-west. The footprint's south face is set 14 m north of the main-stem bank and its west face about 22 m east of the North Branch bank, which puts the building on the point and off both waters. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for the modern banks not being the 1835 banks — this ground was filled and wharfed and is now built over, and unlike the west bank there is no street line here to check it against, so treat the along-bank position as the softer of the two axes. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the main stem, from 'a two-story house ... fronting the river'. On a point the river is on two sides: a bearing of about 215, fronting the confluence and Wolf Point across the water, is equally arguable and would rotate the building about 35 degrees. Local-origin normalization for the reconstructed adjacent compound translates the origin(-6,+5)m in the retained180-degree footprint frame, equivalent to UTM(+6,-5)m. This keeps the tall range's wall box and six front opening world positions unchanged while moving the low core beside it; it does not add a surveyed location. The old20 m placement uncertainty and facade bearing remain. Roof-joint vertices and fractional flue station are governed by the end-route limits, not a whole-mesh equality claim.
placement.symbolic_location: North bank at the forks, on the point of land between the North Branch and the main stem, directly opposite Wolf Point.
